messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo had spent decades moving with fluid certainty. Then came the rain-slicked curve on Route 9, the hydroplane, and the sickening lurch as the passenger door crumpled inward. Glass rained across his lap. When the other driver’s engine cut out, Mateo sat frozen, the smell of burnt rubber thick in his throat, convinced he would never walk again. He couldn’t explain it to his wife, Elena, that night. The image stayed locked behind his eyes, a tight, wordless knot that refused to unravel. In the weeks that followed, Mateo paced the studio floors, his eyes darting to emergency doors the moment he crossed the threshold. Every time he entered a rehearsal room, his gaze locked onto the nearest exit. This hypervigilance acted as a direct trigger for the event itself. Because he was so attuned to danger, the moment he heard a car door slam on the street below, the nonverbal memory of the crush would flood his system, and the sharp sounds of the airbag and bending metal would echo in his head. Each time those sounds and the accompanying shame rushed up, Mateo’s only recourse was to deliberately shut down. He forced his mind to leave his body until the images faded. To keep the silence at bay, he delayed sleep, staying up until three in the morning. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, telling himself that occupying his hands would keep the past buried. The habit only kept the memories jagged. By suppressing his thoughts and fragmenting his rest, Mateo denied his brain the chance to process the event. Instead of settling, the nonverbal memories grew heavier, and the auditory recalls became more frequent, returning uninvited whenever he allowed himself stillness. He began to interpret his exhaustion and emotional numbness as permanent damage. The deliberate blanking out and sleepless nights widened the gap between him and his former self. He came to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, convinced that the event had hollowed him out and left him incapable of the calm he once took for granted. That certainty only deepened the dread. Because he was convinced he couldn’t stop bad things from happening, his nervous system stayed permanently wired to scan for danger. His character blame—telling himself the accident happened because of the sort of person he was—fed a cycle of horror and guilt. When he felt those negative emotions spike, they reinforced his original fear, making him more likely to flinch at unexpected touches and track the exits. The constant alertness became its own prison. Elena would place a hand on his shoulder, and he would react with alarm so violently she would pull back. Over time, the perpetual threat monitoring convinced him that he was fundamentally unsafe and inherently flawed. Every flinch and exit count became proof that bad things were inevitable, and that his own nature was the reason he could never trust the world again. The cycle tightened over months. He stopped teaching advanced classes, citing a knee issue, but the real reason was the studio’s narrow backstage corridors and the way dancers still approached him with quick pats on the back. The avoidance cost him his livelihood and pulled Elena away. What finally brought Mateo to my office was a night he couldn’t suppress through. He walked past a car with flashing hazard lights, heard the rhythmic blinker, and experienced a full-body freeze. He sits on the edge of my couch now, afraid that if he stops holding himself together, he will shatter. He hopes, quietly, for a way to trust his own skin and step through a door without counting the exits.
